1030.title: Darshan: the deity looks back
1030.hook: the temple curtain opens, and a crowd leans in to see the deity and be seen
1030.carry: darshan: you see the deity, and are seen
1030.tomorrow: How does the Gita say to sit?
1030.howItsDone: Temple-goers speak of going for darshan, the sight of the deity present in the murti, which in some temples comes at set times when the curtain is opened and a lamp is offered; many devotees describe it as seeing and being seen.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THIRTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, trataka as dharana you can see: dharana: the mind held on one beloved form.
screen: `TRATAKA.` · `DHARANA: THE MIND HELD ON ONE BELOVED FORM.`

segments.voice: Evening at a temple. A small crowd stands packed in front of a closed curtain, shoes left at the door, hands holding flowers and little plates of sweets. Bells. Then the curtain is drawn aside, the lamp is lifted, and there is the image of the deity, dressed and garlanded, eyes wide. Nobody in the crowd looks away. Some fold their hands. A grandfather lifts a small boy higher so he can see. This is darshan. When the thing you gaze at is not a mark on a wall, what changes?
screen: `THE CURTAIN IS DRAWN ASIDE.` → `A CROWD LEANS IN TO SEE.` → `WHAT IF THE MARK IS SACRED?`

segments.voice: Darshan means seeing, or a sight. In temple worship it names the moment of beholding the deity in the image, the murti. People go to the temple for darshan the way they'd go to visit family. And the teaching underneath is this: for the devotee, God is truly present in the murti, so darshan isn't only looking. As many devotees describe it, the deity is also looking back. The worshipper sees, and is seen. That's why a murti's eyes are so wide, and why in many temples the eyes of a new image are the last part to be opened, in a rite of their own. The Bhagavad Gita has a scene about the limits of that seeing. In chapter eleven, Arjuna asks Krishna to show him his supreme form. And Krishna answers, in paraphrase: you cannot see me with these eyes of yours. I give you a divine eye. Behold my power. Then the vision comes, vast and blazing, more than Arjuna can hold, and he begs to see the familiar, gentle form again. Many teachers read the murti in that light: God, who is more than any eye can hold, takes a form a person can look at, and lets himself be seen. Some who practice trataka choose a sacred image as their point. The method stays the same: a steady gaze, a gentle return. But the gaze is now attention offered to someone. Teachers differ: some keep trataka to a flame, others welcome a sacred image.
screen: `DARSHAN: SEEING, AND BEING SEEN.` · `GOD PRESENT IN THE MURTI.` · `ARJUNA IS GIVEN A DIVINE EYE.` · `A FORM YOU CAN LOOK AT.` · then, large: `THE IMAGE LOOKS BACK.`

segments.voice: If you keep a sacred image, a deity, a symbol, a photo of a teacher, set it at eye level; if not, a flame or a simple mark is just as good. Rest the eyes on it softly, blinking when you need to, and if it's an image that matters to you, let the gaze feel like a greeting rather than a stare. When the eyes tire, close them and hold what stays, then look again.
Trataka. A still gaze at one small point. Today, its neighbor darshan, where the gaze rests on a sacred image, and the worshipper sees and is seen.
screen: `TRATAKA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: darshan: you see the deity, and are seen. The image, this time, looks back. Rest well.

1031.title: The tortoise draws in its limbs
1031.hook: Arjuna asks how a person of steady wisdom sits, and Krishna answers with a tortoise
1031.carry: pratyahara: senses drawn in like the tortoise
1031.tomorrow: What does a steady eye see in everyone?
1031.howItsDone: Many Hindus who meditate or sit for puja begin by drawing the senses in, eyes lowered and resting, following the Gita's picture of the tortoise and its instructions for sitting; yoga teachers call this drawing-in pratyahara.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THIRTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, trataka met darshan: you see the deity, and are seen. The image looked back.
screen: `TRATAKA.` · `DARSHAN: YOU SEE, AND ARE SEEN.`

segments.voice: The battlefield, before the fighting. Arjuna has just heard Krishna describe a person whose wisdom is steady, and he asks the most practical question in the whole Gita. In paraphrase: what does such a person look like? How do they speak? How do they sit? How do they walk? He doesn't want a theory. He wants to see it. And Krishna's answer begins with an animal nobody expects on a battlefield: a tortoise.
screen: `ARJUNA: HOW DO THEY SIT?` → `HOW DO THEY WALK?` → `KRISHNA ANSWERS: A TORTOISE.`

segments.voice: In chapter two, Krishna answers with a picture. In paraphrase: when a person draws the senses back from the things of the senses, the way a tortoise draws in its limbs on every side, that person's wisdom is steady. A tortoise doesn't hate the world. It just doesn't have to be pulled by every sound. It can draw in, and come out again. Yoga teachers often link this verse to pratyahara, Patanjali's word for drawing the senses in. Then, in chapter six, Krishna answers the how-do-they-sit part almost literally. A clean place, a seat neither too high nor too low. In paraphrase: holding the body, head and neck straight and still, gazing at the tip of one's own nose, and not looking around in any direction. The teacher Shankara reads it as if looking at the nose tip: eyes lowered and resting, not crossed. Trataka so far has needed a flame or an image out there. This gaze brings the point home. And the very next verse says why. In paraphrase: calm, fearless, the mind held steady, let the yogi sit with the mind on me, intent on me. So the senses aren't drawn in to make an empty room. They're drawn in so the mind can rest on God. That's the teaching: senses turned home, heart turned toward the Lord. Today the pull is a phone that lights up every few minutes, a feed built never to end. The Gita's answer isn't to hate the phone. It's the tortoise: draw in, rest the mind on God, and come back out when you choose.
screen: `THE TORTOISE DRAWS IN ITS LIMBS.` · `PRATYAHARA: THE SENSES DRAWN IN.` · `HEAD AND NECK STILL, EYES LOWERED.` · `SIT WITH THE MIND ON ME.` · then, large: `TURNED HOME, TURNED TOWARD GOD.`

segments.voice: Sit upright, head and neck easy and straight, and let the eyes lower, half closed, resting as if looking toward the tip of the nose: no crossing, no strain, just no roaming. Picture the tortoise drawing in its limbs, and let sounds and thoughts come and go without chasing them. If you pray, let the mind rest on a name of God you love; if not, rest it on the breath at the nostrils. If the eyes ache, let them simply close.
Trataka. A still gaze at one small point. Today the point comes home: the senses drawn in like a tortoise's limbs, the eyes resting toward the tip of the nose.
screen: `TRATAKA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: pratyahara: senses drawn in like the tortoise. Draw in, then turn toward God. See you tomorrow.

1032.title: The same self in every being
1032.hook: on the steps at Varanasi, the great teacher Shankara tells a man to move aside, and the man's question stops him
1032.carry: sama-darshana: one self in every being
1032.tomorrow: Why does a yoga book begin with Shiva?
1032.howItsDone: Many Hindus speak of seeing God, or the one Self, in every being, and the story of Shankara and the chandala at Varanasi is often told alongside the Gita's sama-darshana to teach it.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THIRTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, trataka came home with the tortoise: pratyahara, the senses drawn in, so the mind can rest on God.
screen: `TRATAKA.` · `PRATYAHARA: SENSES DRAWN IN LIKE THE TORTOISE.`

segments.voice: Varanasi, early morning, the stone steps down to the Ganga. The young teacher Shankara is walking down to bathe, his students around him. Coming up the narrow lane is a man his society treated as outcaste, a chandala, with four dogs at his heels. Shankara calls out the old command: move aside, keep your distance. The man doesn't move. He asks a question instead, and it stops the great teacher where he stands.
screen: `VARANASI, THE STEPS TO THE GANGA.` → `MOVE ASIDE, SAYS THE TEACHER.` → `THE MAN ASKS A QUESTION.`

segments.voice: In the telling handed down with a short poem credited to Shankara, the Manisha Panchakam, the man asks, in paraphrase: what do you want moved away from what? This body from that body, both made of food? Or the Self from the Self, which is the same in both? Shankara, the story goes, bows to him and says that whoever sees this way is his teacher, whatever their birth. Many tellers add that the man was Shiva himself. What Shankara is caught out on is the Gita's own teaching. In chapter six, Krishna describes the one whose mind has become steady in yoga. In paraphrase: such a person sees the Self, the atman, abiding in all beings, and all beings in the Self, and sees the same everywhere. The Sanskrit is sama-darshana: same-seeing. Then Krishna makes it personal: whoever sees me everywhere, and everything in me, I am not lost to them, and they are not lost to me. Two verses later he gives that evenness a heart. In paraphrase: the one who, by the measure of one's own self, sees pleasure or pain in every being as the same, that yogi is held to be the highest. Shankara's commentary reads it plainly: as pain is unwelcome to me, so it is to every being. So this week's steady gaze was never only about a candle. It trains the eyes to look at a stranger, a rival, someone who was rude, and see the same Self looking back. An even gaze isn't a cold one.
screen: `BODY FROM BODY, OR SELF FROM SELF?` · `SHANKARA BOWS.` · `THE SELF IN ALL, ALL IN THE SELF.` · `OTHERS' PAIN AS YOUR OWN.` · then, large: `ONE SELF IN EVERY BEING.`

segments.voice: Rest the gaze on one small point, a flame or a mark, for a little while, blinking when you need to. Then let the gaze soften and widen, without moving the eyes, until it takes in the whole room, and look at all of it with the same calm you gave the point. Bring to mind one person you find hard, and if you pray, greet the same Self in them silently; if not, simply wish them well.
Trataka. A still gaze at one small point. Teachers read the Gita's even gaze as where that calm leads: resting on every being the same.
screen: `TRATAKA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: sama-darshana: one self in every being. Tomorrow, the hands. I'll be here tomorrow.

1033.title: The fish who overheard Shiva
1033.hook: Shiva teaches Parvati the secret of yoga on a lonely shore, and a fish in the water hears every word
1033.carry: the seals that wake the goddess within
1033.tomorrow: Why join your palms for God and for Nani?
1033.howItsDone: In hatha yoga, mudras such as mahamudra and the bandhas are learned from a teacher as whole-body practices; the Nath tradition honors Shiva as Adinatha, the first teacher, and Matsyendranath as the first human guru.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THIRTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday closed trataka with sama-darshana: one Self in every being, even the man told to move aside. Today the eyes rest, and the hands begin.
screen: `TRATAKA.` · `SAMA-DARSHANA: ONE SELF IN EVERY BEING.`

segments.voice: A lonely shore. Shiva is teaching Parvati the secret of yoga: how the body itself can become a path to God. In one telling, Parvati drifts off to sleep. But someone is still listening. In the water just off the shore, a fish, or in some versions a boy swallowed by one, has heard every word. When Shiva notices, he blesses the listener, who becomes Matsyendranath, the lord of fish, remembered as the first human teacher of hatha yoga.
screen: `SHIVA TEACHES PARVATI ON A LONELY SHORE.` → `A FISH HEARS EVERY WORD.` → `MATSYENDRA, THE FIRST TEACHER.`

segments.voice: The Nath yogis tell this story, and the Hatha Yoga Pradipika, the old hatha manual, keeps its spirit. It opens with a bow to Adinatha, the first lord, a name for Shiva, as the one who taught hatha yoga. Its list of masters begins with Adinatha and then Matsyendra. In this tradition, hatha yoga comes from Shiva. Its third chapter is on the mudras. In Sanskrit, mudra can mean a seal, a stamp. The chapter begins with a picture. In paraphrase: as the lord of serpents holds up the earth, so all the practices of yoga rest on kundalini. Then it says why the seals matter. In paraphrase: the goddess lies asleep at the door of Brahman, so practice the mudras with every effort to wake her. That's the teaching. Many Hindu traditions hold that Shakti, the divine power, lives in the body itself, coiled and asleep, and hatha teachers describe the path as waking her to rise and meet Shiva. The body isn't in the way of God. It's where Shiva and Shakti meet. The mudras in that chapter are whole-body seals, not finger shapes: mahamudra, the great seal, with one heel pressed in, the other leg stretched out, the hands holding the foot, the chin drawn down; and the bandhas, locks at the throat, the belly and the root. The text guards them as secret, and they are learned from a teacher, not from a page. So when a class today calls hatha just stretching, the book begins somewhere else: with Shiva, and a goddess waiting to wake.
screen: `THE BOOK BOWS FIRST TO SHIVA.` · `MUDRA: A SEAL.` · `THE GODDESS ASLEEP AT BRAHMAN'S DOOR.` · `MAHAMUDRA, AND THE LOCKS.` · then, large: `WHERE SHIVA AND SHAKTI MEET.`

segments.voice: Sit upright on a cushion or a chair, spine tall, hands resting on the knees. Draw the chin down just a little, without strain, and let the whole body settle into one steady shape, like a seal pressed into wax. Leave the great seal and the stronger locks for a teacher. If you pray, bow inwardly to Shiva, the first teacher, with Om Namah Shivaya; if not, simply rest in the shape and the breath.
The mudras. Seals: shapes of the hands or the whole body, which the hatha texts say help wake the goddess asleep within.
screen: `THE MUDRAS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the seals that wake the goddess within. The body is where Shiva and Shakti meet. Until tomorrow.

1034.title: Arjuna joins his palms
1034.hook: before God's universal form, Arjuna joins his palms; at an arrivals gate, a grandmother does the same
1034.carry: anjali: one bow for God, elders and guests
1034.tomorrow: Why does Shiva teach without a word?
1034.howItsDone: In Hindu homes and temples, people greet the deity, elders, teachers and guests with anjali, palms joined at the chest, often with the words namaste or namaskar and a slight bow of the head.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THIRTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seals that wake the goddess within: the body as the place where Shiva and Shakti meet.
screen: `THE MUDRAS.` · `THE SEALS THAT WAKE THE GODDESS WITHIN.`

segments.voice: The arrivals gate at an airport, late in the evening. A tired young man comes through the sliding doors pulling a suitcase. An older woman at the rail sees him, and before she hugs him, before she says his name, she presses her palms together in front of her chest and dips her head. He does it back. Then the hug. Two seconds, maybe less, and nobody around them notices. That small shape of the hands is a mudra, so familiar it's easy to forget it is one.
screen: `THE ARRIVALS GATE, LATE.` → `PALMS TOGETHER, A DIP OF THE HEAD.` → `A MUDRA, HIDING IN PLAIN SIGHT.`

segments.voice: The gesture has a name: anjali. Two palms joined, fingers pointing up, usually held at the chest, sometimes at the forehead. Anjali can also mean the cupped hollow of two hands, the shape you'd make to carry water or flowers as an offering. So the joined palms carry a sense of offering. And namaste? That's not the gesture. It's the words said with it: namas, a bow; te, to you. Now watch the Bhagavad Gita use this mudra at its most overwhelming moment. In chapter eleven, Arjuna has been given the divine eye and sees Krishna's universal form, vast, blazing, with many faces and eyes. The text tells us what his body does. In paraphrase: filled with wonder, his hair standing on end, Arjuna bowed his head, joined his palms, and spoke. Later, trembling, palms still joined, he bows again and speaks in a choking voice, bowing to Krishna in front, behind, on every side. Notice what the text shows first. Not Arjuna's thoughts. His hands. Before God, the hands go first. And here's the teaching that carries that bow off the battlefield. The Taittiriya Upanishad sends its students home with a list, in paraphrase: let your mother be a god to you, your father a god, your teacher a god, your guest a god. That's why the same joined palms greet the murti in the shrine and the grandmother at the door. In this teaching, the divine is honored in the people in front of you, and anjali is how the hands say it.

1035.title: The silent teacher under the banyan
1035.hook: under a banyan tree, old students sit before a young teacher who says nothing, and their doubts are gone
1035.carry: chin mudra: the small self meets the great
1035.tomorrow: Why is breath more than air?
1035.howItsDone: Practitioners sit in meditation with chin or jnana mudra, thumb and index finger touching and the hands resting on the knees; images of Dakshinamurti show him seated beneath a banyan tree with his hand in this mudra.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THIRTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mudras and anjali: one bow for God, elders and guests, the way Arjuna joined his palms.
screen: `THE MUDRAS.` · `ANJALI: ONE BOW FOR GOD, ELDERS AND GUESTS.`

segments.voice: How strange, an old Sanskrit verse begins. Under a banyan tree sit the students, and they are old. Their teacher is young. And the teacher's lecture is silence. Yet the students' doubts are cut away. The teacher in that verse is Dakshinamurti, Shiva as the teacher. In images of him beneath the tree, one hand is raised, and in that hand the thumb and the first finger touch to make a small circle. He doesn't explain it. In the verse, the silence is enough.
screen: `OLD STUDENTS. A YOUNG TEACHER.` → `THE LECTURE IS SILENCE.` → `ONE HAND, A SMALL CIRCLE.`

segments.voice: The shape is simple. The tip of the index finger meets the tip of the thumb. The other three fingers stay straight, relaxed. It's called chin mudra, the seal of consciousness, or jnana mudra, the seal of knowledge. Lineages use the two names a little differently, sometimes by whether the palm faces up or down, but the finger shape is the same. Teachers read the shape like a sentence. In one common reading, the thumb stands for the Supreme, Brahman. The index finger, the one we point with, stands for the individual self, always pointing outward at this and that. When the index finger bends and touches the thumb, the small self meets the great one. And the three fingers left standing? Some teachers say they are the three gunas, the qualities that make up the world. Others say they are the three states this path spent time with not long ago: waking, dreaming, deep sleep. Either way, in that reading the circle is made apart from the three, and the meeting happens beyond them. That's why it suits Dakshinamurti. Some readers say the students are old because they've studied everything and heard every argument. What finally answers them isn't another argument. It's a hand, held still, showing the meeting instead of describing it. The Taittiriya Upanishad says something similar about its own subject: it's where words turn back, unable to reach it. In the verse's picture, the silence isn't because there's nothing to say, but because this is something better shown. And the hand can show it on a meditation seat, palm resting on the knee, as easily as under a banyan tree.
screen: `THUMB AND FIRST FINGER MEET.` · `THE SMALL SELF BENDS TO THE GREAT.` · `THREE FINGERS: GUNAS, OR THREE STATES.` · `SHOWN, NOT DESCRIBED.` · then, large: `THE LECTURE IS SILENCE.`

segments.voice: Sit upright, rest the backs of the hands on the knees or thighs, and let the tip of each index finger meet the tip of the thumb, lightly, the other three fingers straight but soft. Let the breath settle and say nothing, even inside. If thoughts start explaining, let them go and come back to the touch of the two fingertips.
The mudras. Today, chin mudra, the seal of consciousness: thumb and first finger joined, read by teachers as the small self bowing to the great, shown in silence.

1036.title: The quarrel of the senses
1036.hook: speech, eye, ear and mind each claim to be the best, until the breath begins to leave
1036.carry: prana: breath is life, chief of the senses
1036.tomorrow: Why does the god raise an open palm?
1036.howItsDone: In hatha yoga and before the daily sandhya prayers, many Hindus do alternate-nostril breathing with the right hand, folding the first two fingers and closing each side in turn; breath retention is learned from a teacher.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THIRTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mudras and the silent teacher: chin mudra, the small self meets the great, under a banyan tree.
screen: `THE MUDRAS.` · `CHIN MUDRA: THE SMALL SELF MEETS THE GREAT.`

segments.voice: Long ago, an Upanishad says, the powers of a person had an argument. Speech, the eye, the ear and the mind each said: I am the best. They went to Prajapati, the creator, to settle it. He told them, in paraphrase: the one whose leaving makes the body worst off, that one is the best. So, one by one, they left. Speech went first, and stayed away for a whole year.
screen: `SPEECH, EYE, EAR, MIND: I AM THE BEST.` → `ONE BY ONE, THEY LEAVE.` → `SPEECH GOES FOR A YEAR.`

segments.voice: When speech came back, it asked how the body had managed. In paraphrase: like someone who can't speak, but still breathing, seeing, hearing, thinking. Then the eye left for a year, and the body lived on like the blind. Then the ear, and it lived on like the deaf. Then the mind, and it lived on like a small child. Then the breath began to leave. And the Chandogya Upanishad gives it a picture: like a strong horse tearing up the pegs it was tied to, the breath started tearing all the others up with it. They cried out together, in paraphrase: stay, lord, you are the best of us. That's the teaching. In Hindu thought, breath is prana, life itself, the chief of all the powers, treated as sacred. The Hatha Yoga Pradipika describes alternate-nostril breathing, in paraphrase: in through the left, out through the right; in through the right, out through the left. It says this is how the nadis, the channels of the subtle body, are made clean. The text's version also holds the breath, which teachers say to learn in person. Teachers supply the hand: in some lineages, Vishnu mudra, two fingers folded down, the thumb and ring finger free to close each side in turn. Many who say the daily sandhya prayers begin with pranayama, the right hand at the nose. An app may call this a stress hack. But in the Upanishad's story, breath isn't a tool you use. It's the one that, when it starts to leave, everything else begs to stay.
screen: `THE BODY LIVES ON WITHOUT EACH.` · `THEN THE BREATH BEGINS TO LEAVE.` · `STAY, LORD. PRANA IS LIFE ITSELF.` · `VISHNU MUDRA: ONE NOSTRIL, THEN THE OTHER.` · then, large: `NOT A TOOL. THE CHIEF.`

segments.voice: Sit upright and fold the first two fingers of the right hand into the palm. Close the right nostril with the thumb and breathe in through the left; close the left with the ring finger and breathe out through the right; breathe in through the right, then switch and breathe out through the left: one round. Slow and easy, no holding, no forcing. If you pray, let a name of God ride on each breath; if not, just count the rounds. If the nose is blocked or anything feels uncomfortable, rest the hand and breathe normally.
The mudras. Today, the breathing hand: two fingers folded, thumb and ring finger tending prana, the breath the Upanishad calls chief of all.
